name: characterization-test
intent: Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do.
problem: You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.
context: Applies whenever the subject already runs and can be exercised in a test process or from a test script: untested legacy modules, data transformations and report pipelines, serializers, parsers and code generators, CLI and protocol endpoints, rendering pipelines whose images can be diffed, and dependency or runtime upgrades where the old behaviour is the baseline. The precondition is determinism: volatile parts (timestamps, identifiers, paths, memory addresses, collection order, locale, floating-point formatting) must be normalized or redacted before capture, otherwise the comparison is noise. The pattern is a first move - build the net, then refactor under it - and pairs with a deliberate approval step, because a characterization test does not know which behaviour was intended.
benefits: A regression net exists without a specification: the committed reference encodes actual behaviour, so any unintended change fails a test instead of reaching production unnoticed.
It enables refactoring of legacy code: the suite proves behaviour preservation while structure changes, which is the Feathers use case (pin what it does today, then change how it does it).

Writing the tests is itself discovery: the characterisation surfaces undocumented behaviour, including surprises and bugs, while the code is still cheap to change, and the reference artefact documents what was found.
Coverage for subjects that resist unit testing: one capture of a whole pipeline or produced artefact pins far more behaviour than dozens of hand-written assertions, at a fraction of the setup cost.
A wide stimulus set is affordable: production-derived or recorded inputs can be replayed wholesale, so corner cases nobody remembered get pinned too.
The approved diff becomes reviewable evidence: when behaviour must change on purpose, the change appears as an explicit, reviewable difference in a reference artefact rather than as silence.
Human review is explicit and central: the approval step forces deliberate judgement about behaviour, not rubber-stamping of a status quo (Emily Bache, 2020).

Works with non-deterministic AI/ML outputs when combined with statistical approval thresholds: distributions and embeddings can be compared rather than exact bytes, enabling golden masters for LLM pipelines.
tradeoffs: Golden masters freeze today's bugs as the baseline: the artefact records current behaviour, including behaviour that is wrong, and the approval step quietly legitimizes it unless the defect is fixed (or explicitly annotated) first.

Whole-output artefacts grow until nobody reads them: once a diff is thousands of lines, approval degrades into 'accept everything', and a suite that cannot fail usefully is worse than no suite because it claims coverage.

The comparison is fragile against irrelevant variation: timestamps, ids, iteration order, temporary paths, locale-dependent formatting and image anti-aliasing produce false failures unless they are normalized or redacted, and the normalization is then part of the maintenance burden.

Characterization tests cannot distinguish intended from unintended change: every real behaviour change requires re-approval, so the value of the suite depends entirely on the review discipline around the approval step.

Reference artefacts couple the suite to the current output surface: internal refactoring is safe, but any change of representation (formatting, field order, output medium) means re-recording and re-reviewing the corpus.
Storage and runtime cost: large corpora bloat the repository and slow CI, and the capture runs the subject repeatedly rather than asserting narrowly.

Reference artefacts capture whatever the subject emits, which in a legacy system frequently includes sensitive production data (personal data, tokens, internal hostnames) - a leak vector unless redaction is part of the harness.
AI/LLM outputs are inherently non-deterministic: exact byte comparison produces excessive false failures for stochastic models; statistical or embedding-based comparison is needed, adding complexity.
Approval fatigue sets in when snapshot diffs are large and review is superficial: teams begin approving without reading, defeating the purpose of the net.

participants.responsibility: The existing code exercised exactly as it runs today; it is not modified to make capturing possible (only seams may be opened to reach it).
The recorded, production-derived or generated inputs replayed through the subject; its breadth decides how much behaviour the net actually covers.
Invokes the subject for each stimulus and serializes everything observable: return values, stdout and stderr, produced files, protocol traffic, rendered images.
Removes or masks volatile and sensitive parts (timestamps, ids, paths, addresses, ordering, locale) so that a comparison failure means a behavioural change, not noise.
The committed reference output that encodes the behaviour to be preserved and reviewed in version control.
Re-captures, applies the same normalization and compares with the approved artefact, reporting the first meaningful difference; it never writes the reference.
The only place behaviour may change: a human (or a dedicated, gated job) inspects the received output and promotes it to approved, recording why the behaviour changed.
Measures which parts of the subject the stimulus set exercised, so the team knows what the net covers before refactoring.
For non-deterministic outputs (LLM, ML inference), applies statistical or embedding-based comparison instead of exact byte diff; thresholds determine pass/fail with fallback to human review.

use_cases: Before refactoring an untested legacy module: capture outputs for a corpus of inputs, restructure the code, and require the reference artefacts to stay identical.
Data processing and batch jobs: pin how representative input files are transformed into output files or reports, so the nightly job can be changed safely.
Serializers, formatters and code generators: pin the emitted text or structured output for representative documents, with a redaction step for volatile values.
Rendering and UI pipelines: pin generated images (screenshot goldens) or rendered text output with an approval workflow and a visual diff tool.
CLI and protocol behaviour: pin stdout, stderr and exit codes, or request/response bytes, for a set of recorded invocations.
Dependency or runtime upgrades: pin behaviour before the upgrade and re-run afterwards, so only intended differences have to be reviewed.
Production defect triage: replay the failing production input into a new reference artefact, then fix the defect against that regression test.

AI/LLM output regression testing: pin model responses to a curated golden dataset; on model or prompt change, compare distributions, embedding similarity, or token-level diffs against the baseline rather than requiring exact matches (LLM eval pipelines, 2024-2026).
Generated code verification: pin the exact output of OpenAPI client generators, GraphQL type generators, SDK wrappers, or database migration previews so formatting and structural changes are caught.
Database schema migration testing: capture the before/after output of migration scripts for a set of schema variants, approving only intentional structural differences.

Computer vision pipeline regression: pin bounding-box distributions or classification confidence vectors from CV models across runs; statistical comparison prevents flaky failures from minor pixel noise.
Smart contract and blockchain output regression: pin deterministic contract outputs for a given input state; any divergence in on-chain behaviour is immediately visible (Nexlify case, 2025).

Database-engine regression suites: PostgreSQL's pg_regress replays each sql/*.sql script and diffs results/*.out against committed golden files in expected/*, with variant comparison files and a resultmap absorbing known platform differences (locale, float formatting, row ordering).

Compiler test corpora: LLVM's lit/FileCheck pins emitted IR and machine code by piping compiler output to FileCheck, which verifies CHECK directives committed inside each test file across the whole input corpus.
ORM query-change detection: ApprovalTests.Ruby's verify_sql approves the SQL an ActiveRecord call emits, so a gem or framework upgrade that silently rewrites generated queries fails the suite.
avoid_when: The subject is new code: write assertion-based tests against the intended contract instead (test-first), because a characterisation of whatever got built is weaker than a statement of what it should do.

Behaviour is genuinely undefined, nondeterministic or concurrency-dependent and cannot be normalized or serialized by policy: a golden master then pins noise, and targeted assertions or property-based tests serve better.
The subject is a small, well-understood pure function: a handful of example-based assertions documents intent more clearly and costs less than a reference file plus an approval workflow.

The output is so large or volatile that no reviewer will read the diff: an accept-everything golden master is worse than no suite, because it claims coverage that does not exist; pick targeted invariants instead.

The code is about to be replaced wholesale with a new contract (throw-away migrations, planned rewrites): pinning today's behaviour mostly encodes what is being deleted; test the new contract instead.

Outputs require exact byte-match comparison for inherently stochastic systems (e.g. LLMs at temperature > 0): exact-match golden masters generate excessive false failures; statistical or embedding-based comparison is required instead.
anti_patterns: Golden and forget: reference files are committed once and never read again; runs end with a blanket update flag, so the suite can no longer detect any regression.
Bug as law: a known defect is pinned and the suite declared green, after which the golden master argues against the fix and reviewers defend the reference instead of the correction.
Oversized dumps: a whole application state, page or log is captured into one reference, so a one-character change produces thousands of diff lines and the approval step becomes meaningless.
Nondeterministic capture: unredacted timestamps, identifiers, hash-map ordering, temporary paths or memory addresses inside the reference, producing a flaky test that is eventually disabled.
Characterization as requirement: treating an accidental behaviour as a permanent contract, so the accident outlives the reason it happened.
Pinning internals: snapshotting private data structures or call sequences rather than observable behaviour, which breaks on every refactoring and destroys trust in the net.
Leaking production data: references committed straight from captured traffic with personal or secret values still inside.
Snapshot update in a separate PR: the code change and the approved artefact are decoupled, removing the context a reviewer needs to evaluate whether the behavioural change was intentional.
Exact-match on LLM outputs: requiring byte-identical outputs from a stochastic model at non-zero temperature produces chronic CI flakiness and trains teams to rubber-stamp approvals.
Cross-OS shared snapshots: artefacts created on one operating system produce spurious failures on others due to line endings, font rendering, or anti-aliasing differences.
design_principles: Observed behaviour is the specification of record for existing code: write the tests against what the system does today, then change it under that net (Feathers).
Separate detection from approval: the comparator may fail, only a deliberate reviewed step may change the baseline.
Invariant over accidental: compare the stable essence of the output and normalize or redact everything that legitimately varies.
Safety net before surgery: refactor only while the characterization suite is green, and know its coverage before trusting it.
Proportionate artefacts: keep reference files small enough to be read and diffed in code review, because an unreadable baseline cannot be approved.
One explicit mode switch: recording is a local, deliberate act; verification is the only mode a build server may run.
Approval is iterative, not archival: treat the reference as a reviewed behaviour, not a precious artefact — it can and should be updated when behaviour changes on purpose.
For AI/ML outputs, compare distributions not bytes: exact-match comparison is a false friend for non-deterministic outputs; statistical or embedding-based thresholds are the appropriate oracle.
best_practices: Start from real inputs: replay redacted production traffic or previously recorded corpora, then add boundary cases the corpus does not reach.
Redact rather than delete: masks for timestamps, identifiers, paths and ordering keep the structure of the output visible while making the comparison deterministic.
Keep one reference artefact per logical case, as small as the observation allows, and prefer normalized structured text over whole-system dumps.
Run CI in verify mode only: fail on mismatches, missing references and references no test uses any more, and never allow writes on the build server.
Review approvals like code: the artefact diff is the change, so approve file by file and record in the commit or pull request why the behaviour moved.
Measure coverage of the characterized code before refactoring, and add stimuli for the paths the corpus missed.
Keep known defects visible in an issue or an explicitly marked test rather than only inside a green reference file.
Delete obsolete references when cases disappear, and re-approve deliberately after each intended behaviour change.
Use environment normalization: fix TZ, locale and line-ending settings in CI to prevent cross-developer-machine false failures.
Pair approvals with targeted assertions: approve the full output but assert key invariants separately so failure is self-explanatory without reading the diff.
Version-control the normalizer alongside the artefacts: normalization logic changes can silently break the comparison; treat it as production code.
For generated code, approve after formatting: capture the exact text the consumer would see, including the same formatter the production pipeline uses.
Govern snapshots with policy: set line-count thresholds, require reviewer notes for oversized diffs, and enforce CODEOWNERS on snapshot directories.
For AI/LLM pipelines, use hybrid graders: deterministic rule-based checks (format, schema, required-fields) catch structural regressions; model-based judges catch semantic drift.
Run mutation analysis on the characterization suite itself: verify the net actually kills mutants before trusting it as a safety net.
Classify every captured field as stable or unstable at write time: unstable fields (timestamps, UUIDs, durations) must be normalized or scrubbed before the artefact is committed.
sources: Michael Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code (Prentice Hall, 2004) - characterization tests: pin the actual behaviour of existing code before changing it, because there is no specification to test against.

https://approvaltests.com/ - Approval Tests: take a snapshot of the results and confirm they have not changed; Approvals.verify(...) with explicit approve and re-approve steps (Llewellyn Falco and contributors).

https://github.com/approvals/ApprovalTests.cpp - 'Also known as Golden Master Tests or Snapshot Testing': single-header approval library integrating with GoogleTest, Catch2, doctest, CppUTest and Boost.Test.
https://insta.rs/docs/quickstart/ - snapshot review workflow for Rust: .snap.new files, cargo insta review/test, INSTA_UPDATE modes, inline snapshots and CI detection.
https://jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing - snapshot artefacts committed alongside the code, updateSnapshot/-u re-recording, inline snapshots and property matchers.

Emily Bache, 'Why we should be saying Approval Testing instead of Golden Master' (ProAgile, 2020): argues for dropping 'Golden Master' terminology in favour of 'Approval Testing' which foregrounds human judgement in the review step.

Marko Lauronen, 'Characterization Testing — refactoring legacy code with confidence' (Cloudamite, 2024): practical step-by-step guide covering determinism preparation via injectable seams, coverage-guided corpus expansion, and incremental refactoring.

Helpmetest.com, 'Snapshot Testing in CI/CD Pipelines: Setup and Best Practices' (2025): CI-specific challenges including jest --ci behaviour, TZ normalization, parallel runner integrity, and automated update workflows.

Pramod Dutta, 'Approval Testing and Golden Master Testing Guide' (QASkills.sh, 2026): fixture selection, normalizer design, JSON/text/image approvals, generated code verification, diff quality, and redaction.
QASkills.sh, 'Snapshot Testing Governance Guide' (2026): snapshot tiering, update vs fix decision tree, sanitization patterns, pruning rules, and anti-pattern catalogue.
jlevy/tbd, 'Golden Testing Guidelines' (GitHub): stable/unstable field classification, switchable mock modes (live vs mocked), CLI for AI agent testing, layered assertions alongside raw diff.

Ankush Choudhary Johal, 'Golden Master Approval: Snapshot Testing Hypothesis 2025' (johal.in, 2025): statistical extension for AI/LLM outputs using edit distance, embedding cosine similarity, KS-tests, and ML classifiers for probabilistic approval.

Galtea.ai, 'Automated LLM Evaluation: Building a CI/CD quality gate that actually runs' (2026): llm-eval-ci tool; deterministic heuristic graders; golden dataset versioning; regression gate with per-grader thresholds; GitHub Actions integration.

AI Programming Manual, 'AI Evals in Production' (2026): golden dataset design, CI regression gates for prompts and model changes, hybrid scoring, production observability, and a 30-day rollout playbook.

Kurt Zoglmann, 'Golden-Output Regression Test' (Abstractopedia): academic framing of golden-output regression as a characterisation oracle; equivalence-preserving rewrite; observable-behaviour boundary; pairing with metamorphic testing.
Mitchell Hashimoto, 'Testing with Golden Files' (mitchellh.com/writing): practitioner's guide to golden file testing widely cited in Go and infrastructure communities.

https://michaelfeathers.silvrback.com/characterization-testing - Michael Feathers' own account of characterization testing: write tests that describe how the code does behave, then rename them to reflect what was observed.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characterization_test - canonical definition: tests describing the actual behaviour of existing (often legacy) code to protect it from unintended changes; coined by Feathers, equated with Golden Master testing.

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/regress-evaluation.html - PostgreSQL's golden-file regression framework in production use: results diffed against expected/*.out, with documented platform-variance handling (floats, locale, row order) as the normalization burden in practice.
https://www.llvm.org/docs/CommandGuide/FileCheck.html - LLVM FileCheck: committed CHECK directives verify tool output in lit regression tests, pinning compiler behaviour across a large input corpus.

https://engineering.ezcater.com/the-case-against-react-snapshot-testing - practitioner critique: whole-output snapshots fail for unrelated changes, developers update them reflexively, and teams reshape components to fit snapshots instead of behaviour.
